1. Captions can be wrong

Stan Scribe turns speech into text automatically, on your device. Automatic captions can miss words, get words wrong, show them late, or show them under the wrong speaker. Accuracy depends on the room, the microphone, accents, overlapping speech and other things the app can't control. The same goes for everything else the app works out on its own: the names it puts on known voices, and its titles, topics, places and summaries.

Do not rely on the app when a mistake could hurt someone or cost something important. That includes emergencies, medical care, legal matters, safety instructions, and anything else where you need every word to be exact. Stan Scribe is not a medical device and does not replace a professional interpreter or captioner.

2. Ask before you caption people

When the app is on, it listens to everyone nearby, not only you. It keeps listening when you switch to another app or lock your iPhone, until you tap Stop. In many places the law says people must agree before their conversation is captured, and in some places everyone in the conversation must agree. The rules differ by country and state.

You are responsible for using the app lawfully. That means:

  • telling people the app is on, and getting their agreement where the law requires it;
  • not using the app to listen to conversations you are not part of, or to listen to anyone in secret;
  • tapping Stop when your conversation is over;
  • setting up a voice profile only for a person who has agreed to it. Some laws, including laws in Illinois, Texas and Washington, treat voiceprints as biometric information.

3. Your conversations are yours

What the app makes stays on your device unless you send it somewhere, and you own it. I have no copy and no access. When you share, export or sync a conversation, or back it up to iCloud, the app or service you send it to has its own terms. Back up or export anything you want to keep: if your device is lost or the app is deleted, I cannot recover it.
